   235	    {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
   236	    (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Submeasurement α d) :
   237	    OneMeasNaimarkLemma α d M := by
   238	  classical
   239	  let auxProj : Option α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (Option α) :=
   240	    fun oa => Matrix.single oa oa 1
   241	  /-
   242	  The prescribed Naimark isometry column:
   243	    `V (|ψ⟩ ⊗ |⊥⟩)
   244	      = ∑_a √(M_a)|ψ⟩ ⊗ |a⟩ + √(I - ∑_a M_a)|ψ⟩ ⊗ |⊥⟩`,
   245	  encoded by `oneMeasNaimarkColumn M`.  Concretely, this matrix is
   246	  supported only on the input `none = ⊥` slice.
   247	  -/
   248	  let V : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (d × Option α) := oneMeasNaimarkColumn M
   249	  /-
   250	  Extend the isometry column `V` to a unitary `U` on the whole enlarged space.
   251	  The dilated projectors are then `U† (I ⊗ |oa⟩⟨oa|) U`.
   252	  -/
   253	  obtain ⟨U, hU⟩ :=
   254	    partialIsometry_to_unitary
   255	      (oneMeasNaimarkColumn M) (oneMeasNaimarkInputProj (α := α) (d := d))
   256	      oneMeasNaimarkInputProj_isProj
   257	      (oneMeasNaimarkColumn_mul_inputProj M)
   258	      (oneMeasNaimarkColumn_isometry M)
   259	  let Umat : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (d × Option α) := U
   260	  refine ⟨{
   261	    source := M
   262	    liftedEffect := fun oa =>
   263	      Umatᴴ * Matrix.kronecker (1 : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op d) (auxProj oa) * Umat
   264	    lifted_isProj := ?_
   265	    lifted_sum_le_one := ?_
   266	    expectation_preservation := ?_
   267	  }, rfl⟩
   268	  · intro oa
   269	    /-
   270	    `U† (I ⊗ |oa⟩⟨oa|) U` is a projection because `I ⊗ |oa⟩⟨oa|` is, and
   271	    conjugation by a unitary preserves Hermitian idempotents.
   272	    -/
   273	    let P : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (d × Option α) :=
   274	      Matrix.kronecker (1 : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op d) (auxProj oa)
   275	    have hPproj : MIPStarRE.Quantum.IsProj P := by
   276	      exact isProj_kronecker
   277	        ((IsStarProjection.one _))
   278	        (optionBasisProj_isProj oa)
   279	    simpa [Umat, P] using isProj_unitary_conj U hPproj
   280	  · /-
   281	    Since the auxiliary rank-one projectors sum to the identity on `Option α`,
   282	    the lifted family is actually a complete projective measurement, hence in
   283	    particular a submeasurement.
   284	    -/
   285	    have hauxDecomp : ∑ oa : Option α, auxProj oa = auxProj none + ∑ a : α, auxProj (some a) := by

   108	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=

   121	/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
   122	`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper

   124	noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
   125	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
   126	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   127	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)
   128	  let acted := applyOperatorToState M S.ψ
   129	  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re

   131	/-- Alice's marginal Born weight for an answer at a fixed question. -/

   133	    (x : G.QuestionA) (a : G.AnswerA) : ℝ :=
   134	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   135	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) 1

   141	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   142	    heteroKron 1 ((S.B y).effect b)

   147	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB)
   148	    (E : G.AnswerA → G.AnswerB → Prop) [DecidableRel E] : ℝ :=
   149	  ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,

   154	    (x : G.QuestionA) (E : G.AnswerA → Prop) [DecidablePred E] : ℝ :=

   181	        heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)) =
   182	          (1 : Op (S.ιA × S.ιB)) := by
   183	    ext i j
   184	    simp only [Matrix.sum_apply, heteroKron, Matrix.kronecker,
   185	      Matrix.kroneckerMap_apply]
   186	    simp_rw [← Finset.mul_sum, ← Finset.sum_mul]
   187	    rw [show (∑ a : G.AnswerA, (S.A x).effect a i.1 j.1) =
   188	        (1 : Op S.ιA) i.1 j.1 by
   189	      simpa only [Matrix.sum_apply] using congrFun (congrFun (S.A x).sum_eq_one i.1) j.1]

   191	        (1 : Op S.ιB) i.2 j.2 by
   192	      simpa only [Matrix.sum_apply] using congrFun (congrFun (S.B y).sum_eq_one i.2) j.2]

   194	      (Matrix.one_kronecker_one (m := S.ιA) (n := S.ιB) (α := ℂ)) i) j

   225	/-! ## The dilated projective measurement -/
   226	
   227	/-- A one-measurement Naimark dilation of a positive operator valued measure,
   228	chosen once and for all.  It provides orthogonal projections on the enlarged
   229	space `ℂ^{d × Option α}` whose ground-slice compressions are the given effects;
   230	see `references/ldt-paper/orthonormalization.tex:121-159`. -/
   231	noncomputable def naimarkData {α d : Type} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   232	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement α d) : OneMeasNaimarkData α d :=
   233	  Classical.choose (oneMeasNaimark M.toSubmeasurement)
   234	
   235	/-- The chosen dilation dilates the intended measurement. -/
   236	theorem naimarkData_source {α d : Type} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   237	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement α d) :
   238	    (naimarkData M).source = M.toSubmeasurement :=
   239	  Classical.choose_spec (oneMeasNaimark M.toSubmeasurement)
   240	
   241	/-- The dilated projections indexed by genuine answers already sum to at most the
   242	identity, since the projection attached to the adjoined point is positive
   243	semidefinite. -/

   826	/-- Transfer of state-dependent effect bounds.  Every average squared distance

   831	paper `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:612-652`. -/
   832	theorem opFamilyDistSq_naimarkInflation (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   833	    {X γ ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype γ] [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA]
   834	    [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
   835	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → γ → Op ιA) (P : X → γ → Op ιB)
   836	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
   837	    opFamilyDistSq μ
   838	        (fun x c => heteroKron (naimarkInflation (α := α) (M x c))
   839	          (naimarkInflation (α := α) (P x c)))
   840	        (fun x c => heteroKron (naimarkInflation (α := α) (N x c))
   841	          (naimarkInflation (α := α) (P x c)))
   842	        (naimarkDilatedState α ψ) =
   843	      opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x c => heteroKron (M x c) (P x c))
   844	        (fun x c => heteroKron (N x c) (P x c)) ψ := by
   845	  unfold opFamilyDistSq
   846	  congr 1
   847	  funext x
   848	  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun c _ => ?_
   849	  have hkron : ∀ {ρA ρB : Type} [Fintype ρA] [DecidableEq ρA] [Fintype ρB] [DecidableEq ρB]
   850	      (X Y : Op ρA) (Z : Op ρB),
   851	      heteroKron X Z - heteroKron Y Z = heteroKron (X - Y) Z := by
   852	    intro ρA ρB _ _ _ _ X Y Z
   853	    ext p q
   854	    simp [heteroKron, Matrix.kronecker, sub_mul]
   855	  have hinfl : naimarkInflation (α := α) (M x c) - naimarkInflation (α := α) (N x c) =
   856	      naimarkInflation (α := α) (M x c - N x c) := by
   857	    ext p q
   858	    by_cases h : p.2 = none ∧ q.2 = none <;> simp [h]
   859	  rw [hkron, hkron, hinfl, norm_applyOperatorToState_heteroKron_naimarkInflation]

   621	/-- The matrix of a linear isometry of Euclidean spaces in the computational
   622	bases.  Formalization-only support for `thm:ms-rigidity`, blueprint
   623	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`. -/
   624	noncomputable def isometryMatrix {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   625	    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
   626	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') : Matrix ι' ι ℂ :=
   627	  Matrix.toEuclideanLin.symm φ.toLinearMap
   628	
   629	/-- Conjugation by an isometry is conjugation by its matrix. -/
   630	theorem conjIsometry_eq {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   631	    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
   632	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') (M : Op ι) :
   633	    conjIsometry φ M = isometryMatrix φ * M * (isometryMatrix φ)ᴴ := rfl
   634	
   635	/-- The matrix of an isometry acts on vectors as the isometry does. -/
   636	theorem isometryMatrix_mulVec {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   637	    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
   638	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) :
   639	    isometryMatrix φ *ᵥ WithLp.ofLp x = WithLp.ofLp (φ x) := by
   640	  have h : Matrix.toEuclideanLin (isometryMatrix φ) = φ.toLinearMap :=
   641	    Matrix.toEuclideanLin.apply_symm_apply φ.toLinearMap
   642	  have h' : Matrix.toEuclideanLin (isometryMatrix φ) x = φ x := by rw [h]; rfl
   643	  simpa using congrArg WithLp.ofLp h'
   644	
   645	/-- The columns of the matrix of an isometry are the images of the basis
   646	vectors. -/
   647	theorem isometryMatrix_apply {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   648	    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
   649	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') (k : ι') (i : ι) :
   650	    isometryMatrix φ k i =
   651	      φ ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1)) k := by
   652	  have h := congrFun (isometryMatrix_mulVec φ
   653	    ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1))) k
   654	  rw [← h]
   655	  simp [Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct, EuclideanSpace.equiv, eq_comm]
   656	
   657	/-- The matrix of a composite isometry is the product of the two matrices. -/
   658	theorem isometryMatrix_comp {ι κ ν : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   659	    [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ] [Fintype ν] [DecidableEq ν]
   660	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ κ →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ν)
   661	    (E : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κ) :
   662	    isometryMatrix (φ.comp E) = isometryMatrix φ * isometryMatrix E := by
   663	  ext k i
   664	  have h := congrFun (isometryMatrix_mulVec φ
   665	    (E ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1)))) k
   666	  rw [isometryMatrix_apply, Matrix.mul_apply]
   667	  simp only [isometryMatrix_apply E]
   668	  simpa [Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct] using h.symm
   669	
   670	/-- Conjugating by a composite isometry is conjugating twice.  This is how the
   671	ground embeddings of the dilation combine with the local isometries produced by
   672	the self-testing argument of `thm:ms-rigidity`, blueprint
   673	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`. -/
   674	theorem conjIsometry_comp {ι κ ν : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   675	    [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ] [Fintype ν] [DecidableEq ν]
   676	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ κ →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ν)
   677	    (E : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κ) (M : Op ι) :
   678	    conjIsometry (φ.comp E) M = conjIsometry φ (conjIsometry E M) := by
   679	  rw [conjIsometry_eq, conjIsometry_eq, conjIsometry_eq, isometryMatrix_comp]
   680	  simp [Matrix.conjTranspose_mul, Matrix.mul_assoc]

     4	/-!
     5	# A simultaneous projective dilation of a Magic Square strategy
     6	
     7	The rigidity argument for the Magic Square game is stated for an arbitrary
     8	tensor-product strategy, whose measurements are positive operator valued
     9	measures.  The self-testing argument, however, manipulates projections.  This
    10	file removes that discrepancy by dilating an arbitrary strategy to a projective
    11	one without changing any observable quantity.
    12	
    13	Each local Hilbert space `ℂ^ι` is enlarged by one auxiliary register whose
    14	basis is indexed by `Option MsAnswer`, and the original space is identified with
    15	the *ground slice* `ℂ^ι ⊗ |⊥⟩`.  The one-measurement Naimark lemma of the low
    16	individual degree development supplies, for every question separately, a family
    17	of projections on the enlarged space whose compression to the ground slice
    18	returns the original effects; the ancilla is the same for all questions, so the
    19	identification of `ℂ^ι` with the ground slice is a single isometry serving every
    20	question at once.  Folding the deficiency `1 - ∑_a P_a` into one distinguished
    21	answer turns the dilated family into a complete projective measurement without
    22	disturbing the compression, because the original effects already sum to the
    23	identity.
    24	
    25	Since the dilated state is the image of the original state under the two ground
    26	embeddings, every Born probability, and hence the game value and all the
    27	rejection, malformed-answer, cell-consistency and parity masses of the
    28	value-to-parity layer, is unchanged.  Conversely, the local isometries produced
    29	by a rigidity argument applied to the dilated strategy compose with the ground
    30	embeddings to give local isometries of the original strategy, and the
    31	state-dependent norms occurring in the conclusion of `thm:ms-rigidity` transfer
    32	along that composition.
    33	
    34	## References
    35	
    36	The rigidity statement supported here is `thm:ms-rigidity` in
    37	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`, from
    38	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:612-652`,
    39	proved in Coladangelo--Stark, Theorem 6.9.  The dilation reuses the
    40	one-measurement Naimark lemma of
    41	`references/ldt-paper/orthonormalization.tex:121-159`, formalized as
    42	`MIPStarRE.LDT.MakingMeasurementsProjective.oneMeasNaimark`.
    43	-/
    44	
    45	open scoped BigOperators Matrix MatrixOrder ComplexOrder
    46	
    47	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT.MagicSquareRigidity
    48	
    49	open MIPStarRE.LDT MIPStarRE.Quantum

    53	
    54	/-! ## Orthogonality inside a subnormalized family of projections -/
    55	
    56	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`
    57	(blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`).  If an orthogonal projection `P` and a
    58	positive semidefinite operator `Q` satisfy `P + Q ≤ 1`, then `P` annihilates
    59	`Q`.  Indeed `Tr(P Q)` is nonnegative because both operators are positive
    60	semidefinite, while `0 ≤ Tr(P (1 - P - Q)) = -Tr(P Q)` because `1 - P - Q` is
    61	positive semidefinite and `P` is idempotent; so the pairing vanishes and the
    62	product of two positive semidefinite operators with vanishing trace pairing is
    63	zero. -/
    64	theorem mul_eq_zero_of_isProj_of_add_le_one {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    65	    {P Q : Op d} (hP : IsProj P) (hQ : 0 ≤ Q) (hPQ : P + Q ≤ 1) :
    66	    P * Q = 0 := by
    67	  have hrest : (0 : Op d) ≤ 1 - (P + Q) := sub_nonneg.mpr hPQ
    68	  have hexpand : P * (1 - (P + Q)) = -(P * Q) := by
    69	    have hPP : P * P = P := hP.isIdempotentElem
    70	    rw [Matrix.mul_sub, Matrix.mul_add, hPP, Matrix.mul_one]
    71	    abel
    72	  have hle : Complex.re (Matrix.trace (P * Q)) ≤ 0 := by
    73	    have h := trace_mul_nonneg_of_nonneg hP.nonneg hrest
    74	    rw [hexpand] at h
    75	    simpa using h
    76	  have hge : 0 ≤ Complex.re (Matrix.trace (P * Q)) :=
    77	    trace_mul_nonneg_of_nonneg hP.nonneg hQ
    78	  exact mul_eq_zero_of_nonneg_of_trace_mul_eq_zero hP.nonneg hQ (le_antisymm hle hge)
    79	
    80	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`
    81	(blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`).  A finite family of orthogonal
    82	projections whose sum is at most the identity is mutually orthogonal: for two
    83	distinct indices the two projections already sum to at most the identity, so the
    84	previous lemma applies. -/
    85	theorem mul_eq_zero_of_isProj_family {d α : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    86	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] {P : α → Op d} (hP : ∀ a, IsProj (P a))
    87	    (hsum : ∑ a, P a ≤ 1) {a b : α} (hab : a ≠ b) :
    88	    P a * P b = 0 := by
    89	  refine mul_eq_zero_of_isProj_of_add_le_one (hP a) (hP b).nonneg ?_
    90	  refine le_trans ?_ hsum
    91	  have hpair : ∑ c ∈ ({a, b} : Finset α), P c = P a + P b := by
    92	    rw [Finset.sum_pair hab]
    93	  rw [← hpair]
    94	  exact Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg (Finset.subset_univ _)
    95	    (fun c _ _ => (hP c).nonneg)
    96	
    97	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`
    98	(blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`).  The sum of a mutually orthogonal
    99	family of projections is again an orthogonal projection; mutual orthogonality is
   100	supplied by the hypothesis that the sum is at most the identity. -/
   101	theorem isProj_sum_of_isProj_of_sum_le_one {d α : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]

    14	
    15	The arguments apply to arbitrary finite POVMs.  In particular, malformed

    17	`constraintBitOrZero` turn the common answer alphabet into binary outcomes.
    18

    21	The Magic Square game is defined in

    23	and `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:201-222`.  These relations are the
    24	probabilistic input to the rigidity result cited at paper lines 612-652 from
    25	Coladangelo--Stark, Theorem 6.9.

## Reviewer checklist

Use this alongside the blocker
list in the lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference and the [`proof_frontier_review.md`](./proof_frontier_review.md)
checklist for structure fields. For any theorem or lemma that claims a paper
result, ask:

- [ ] **Hypothesis audit.** Does any hypothesis contain (up to `∃`/`∧`) the
      theorem's conclusion? If yes, that's A1 — reject or strengthen.
- [ ] **Definitional audit.** Is the proof `rfl` or a one-line `simp`? If
      yes, does the unfolded definition do the paper's math, or just match
      the shape of the conclusion? The latter is A2.
- [ ] **Domain audit.** Does the function have a fallback branch (`if
      eligible ... else default`)? If yes, does the theorem's signature
      require eligibility? If not, that's A3.
- [ ] **Witness audit.** Does the proof pick `x := default` for an
      existential named after a paper lemma? That's A4 unless the witness
      is genuinely unique-up-to-isomorphism.
- [ ] **Mathlib audit.** Is there a `private lemma` that duplicates a
      Mathlib fact? Run `exact?` / `apply?` / `#find` before accepting it
      (A5).
- [ ] **External-citation audit.** Does the proof consume a `*Statement` /
      `*Witness` / `*Package`? Is there a tracking issue that names its
      grounding plan (A6)?
- [ ] **Paper-faithfulness.** Does the Lean signature match the paper's
      statement, or does Lean sneak in extra hypotheses? Flag divergences
      as ⚠️S in [#1379].

A lemma that passes all of these is a proof. A lemma that fails one is
scaffolding, and should be labelled and tracked as such (don't tag with
`\leanok` until the gap is closed).

## CI prevention

Mechanical detection is possible for many of these patterns:

- **A1 (conclusion-shaped hypothesis).** Use
  `python3 scripts/audit_conclusion_shaped_hypotheses.py --ci` as the current
  report-only tripwire for the PR [#491] inline-existential mutation. It parses
  theorem/lemma headers and warns when an explicit existential hypothesis shares
  the conclusion's salient structure, while printing witness-adapter helpers
  separately. When [#438] lands (`\leanok` ↔ `sorryAx` drift), extend the same
  idea to all `\leanok`-tagged declarations: parse the hypothesis list; if any
  hypothesis's type (modulo `∃`/`∀`/`∧`) contains a prefix of the conclusion
  structure, warn.
- **A2 (definitional sleight).** Grep for `theorem <Name>.* := rfl` where
  `<Name>` has a blueprint `\lean{}` cross-reference. The only allowed cases
  are ones annotated with `@[paper_bookkeeping]` (proposed attribute) or in
  an allow-list.
- **A3 (zero-fallback).** Grep for identifier suffixes `fallback`, `or0`,
  `orDefault`, `placeholder`, `sentinel` in `Defs/*` files. Each should have
  a docstring citing the downstream eligibility precondition.
- **A4 (default witnesses).** Grep `:= default`, `refine ⟨default`, `exact
  ⟨default`, `Classical.arbitrary` inside proof bodies (not typeclass
  definitions). Cross-reference to [#1379]'s witness ledger.
- **A5 (Mathlib bypass).** No reliable CI check, but `audits/` reports
  catch it during per-chapter audits.
- **A6 (external smuggles).** Every new `structure *Statement` without a
  producing theorem should be required to carry a `/-- Grounded by: #NNN
  -/` docstring, enforced by a lint rule over `blueprint/`.

The scripts in `scripts/` (notably `scripts/blueprint_lean_sync.py` and
`scripts/blueprint_leanok_axioms.py`) are the natural home for extensions that
add these checks.

## Reviewer Checklist

Before approving a PR that adds or modifies a structure field in a type named
with a suffix such as `Input`, `Residual`, `BridgeInputs`, `Witness`,
`Statement`, `Conclusion`, or `Obligations`, check the following points.

1. **Classify each new field.** State whether the field is produced in the PR,
   remains an external residual, or is only a bookkeeping conversion.
2. **Name the obligation discharger.** If the field is produced, cite the exact
   Lean theorem that derives it from the paper hypotheses. If no such theorem
   exists, keep the parent mathematical issue open and link a native sub-issue
   for the missing obligation.
3. **Check the blueprint frontier.** For work near `mainFormal`, Section 6,
   self-improvement, orthonormalization, or projectivization, inspect
   `blueprint/dep_graph_document.html` after building the blueprint. The
   remaining open vertices are part of the review context, even when the source
   diff contains no `sorry`.
4. **Reject hidden residual drift.** A theorem that merely moves an assumption
   into a structure field should be described as a conditional helper or a
   remaining obligation, not as proving the paper step.
5. **Review public prose.** Docstrings, module text, PR descriptions, and
   blueprint paragraphs should distinguish obligations proved from the paper
   hypotheses from inputs of conditional helpers and bookkeeping conversions.
6. **Size follow-up tasks by proof leaves.** Prefer issues such as "prove the
   raw Step 3 Cauchy--Schwarz estimate" to issues such as "close the
   self-improvement inputs" when the latter contains several independent
   proof obligations.
7. **Use native sub-issues.** Missing obligations should be linked under the
   correct parent tracker instead of being left only in a PR comment.

## Diagonal and Completion Data

The recent Section 6 and self-improvement work exposed several tracked
proof-obligation structures. They should be reviewed as debt to remove, not as
new source hypotheses to normalize. The recurring ambiguity is that a theorem
may mention diagonal data, completion data, or restricted strategy data while
only repackaging such data as an explicit input.

For any theorem whose name or docstring mentions diagonal consistency,
line-130 data, completion, restricted strategies, or repaired strategy data,
reviewers should ask the following mathematical question:

Does the theorem derive the stated object from the paper hypotheses, or does it
assume that object as a field?

For line 130 of `references/ldt-paper/inductive_step.tex`, in particular,
the paper supplies a cross relation between `G^A` and `G^B`. A Lean theorem
that consumes diagonal strong self-consistency of `G^A` or `G^B` should not be
described as deriving that diagonal input unless it contains the missing
argument.

## Blueprint Tags

Use `\leanok` only when the Lean declaration proves the mathematical assertion
of the blueprint node under the stated hypotheses. If the Lean declaration is a
conditional wrapper or input splitter, then the blueprint should say so
explicitly. It may still cite the declaration with `\lean{...}`, but the prose
must identify the remaining obligation.

When a PR introduces a public auxiliary lemma that is not a named paper
statement, the blueprint should either omit it or cite it as a subordinate
formalization-only support lemma. Do not allow a support lemma to inherit the
status of the paper theorem whose proof will eventually consume it.

## Examples From the Project

- Issue #1110 and the surrounding Section 6 work showed that diagonal and
  line-130 inputs can be made type-correct without proving the diagonal
  obligation. Such declarations must be described as conditional inputs.
- Issue #1109 concerned final-field boundedness. The generalized theorem
  `final_fields_bounded` is a genuine obligation discharger once the SDP dual
  witness satisfies `I <= Z`; the blueprint prose was updated to state that
  hypothesis and the theorem's actual generality.
- Issues #1070 and #1072 are examples of proof-frontier work where individual
  structure fields had to be separated from the mathematical obligation still
  tracked by the parent self-improvement issue.
- Issue #1081 and parent issue #931 illustrate why a parent tracker should stay
  open when a PR only supplies a conditional helper or residual record.

These examples are not special exceptions. They are the model for future review:
identify the mathematical obligation, name the residual when it remains, and
keep the public prose faithful to that distinction.

   433	/-- The real sign `(-1)^b` associated with a binary answer. -/
   434	def bitSign (b : ZMod 2) : ℝ :=
   435	  (-1 : ℝ) ^ b.val
   436	
   437	/-- The binary sign turns addition into multiplication. -/
   438	theorem bit_sign_add (b c : ZMod 2) :
   439	    bitSign (b + c) = bitSign b * bitSign c := by
   440	  unfold bitSign
   441	  rw [ZMod.val_add]
   442	  rw [← neg_one_pow_eq_pow_mod_two]
   443	  exact pow_add _ _ _
   444	
   445	/-- The sign of a three-bit parity is the product of the three signs. -/
   446	theorem bit_sign_sum_fin_three (β : Fin 3 → ZMod 2) :
   447	    bitSign (∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = ∏ k : Fin 3, bitSign (β k) := by
   448	  rw [Fin.sum_univ_three, Fin.prod_univ_three, bit_sign_add, bit_sign_add]
   449	
   450	/-- A binary sign is never zero. -/
   451	theorem bit_sign_ne_zero (b : ZMod 2) : bitSign b ≠ 0 := by
   452	  unfold bitSign
   453	  exact pow_ne_zero _ (by norm_num)
   454	
   455	/-- The product of the three output signs, with malformed constraint answers
   456	assigned zero so that they remain parity failures. -/
   457	def constraintParityProduct : MsAnswer → ℝ
   458	  | .triple β => ∏ k : Fin 3, bitSign (β k)
   459	  | .bit _ => 0
   460	
   461	/-- Failure of the required sign product for one row or column constraint. -/
   462	def ConstraintParityFailure (i : Fin 6) (a : MsAnswer) : Prop :=
   463	  constraintParityProduct a ≠ bitSign (msParity i)
   464	
   465	/-- Equality of the real parity signs is classically decidable on the finite
   466	Magic Square answer alphabet. -/
   467	noncomputable instance (i : Fin 6) : DecidablePred (ConstraintParityFailure i) :=
   468	  fun a => Classical.propDecidable (ConstraintParityFailure i a)
   469	
   470	/-- Every wrong-form constraint answer is included in the parity-failure event. -/
   471	theorem wrong_constraint_answer_implies_parity_failure (i : Fin 6) (a : MsAnswer)
   472	    (ha : wrongConstraintAnswer a = true) : ConstraintParityFailure i a := by
   473	  cases a with
   474	  | triple β => simp [wrongConstraintAnswer] at ha
   475	  | bit γ =>
   476	      unfold ConstraintParityFailure constraintParityProduct
   477	      exact (bit_sign_ne_zero (msParity i)).symm
   478	
   479	/-- Alice's local failure mass for the row or column sign product. -/
   480	noncomputable def aliceParityFailureMass (S : Strategy msGame) (i : Fin 6) : ℝ :=
   481	  aliceEventWeight S (.constraint i) (ConstraintParityFailure i)
   482	
   483	/-- Bob's local failure mass for the row or column sign product. -/
   484	noncomputable def bobParityFailureMass (S : Strategy msGame) (i : Fin 6) : ℝ :=
   485	  bobEventWeight S (.constraint i) (ConstraintParityFailure i)
   486	
   487	/-- Alice's malformed constraint mass is part of her parity-failure mass. -/
   488	theorem alice_constraint_wrong_form_mass_le_parity_failure_mass (S : Strategy msGame)
   489	    (i : Fin 6) : aliceConstraintWrongFormMass S i ≤ aliceParityFailureMass S i := by
   490	  unfold aliceConstraintWrongFormMass aliceParityFailureMass
   491	  rw [← outcome_event_weight_left_eq S (.constraint i) (.var (msConstraintVars i 0))]
   492	  rw [← outcome_event_weight_left_eq S (.constraint i) (.var (msConstraintVars i 0))]
   493	  exact outcome_event_weight_mono S _ _ _ _ fun a _ ha =>
   494	    wrong_constraint_answer_implies_parity_failure i a ha
   495	
   496	/-- Bob's malformed constraint mass is part of his parity-failure mass. -/
   497	theorem bob_constraint_wrong_form_mass_le_parity_failure_mass (S : Strategy msGame)
   498	    (i : Fin 6) : bobConstraintWrongFormMass S i ≤ bobParityFailureMass S i := by
   499	  unfold bobConstraintWrongFormMass bobParityFailureMass
   500	  rw [← outcome_event_weight_right_eq S (.var (msConstraintVars i 0)) (.constraint i)]
   501	  rw [← outcome_event_weight_right_eq S (.var (msConstraintVars i 0)) (.constraint i)]
   502	  exact outcome_event_weight_mono S _ _ _ _ fun _ b hb =>
   503	    wrong_constraint_answer_implies_parity_failure i b hb

   506	    (a b : MsAnswer) (hparity : ConstraintParityFailure i a) :
   507	    msWinPredicate (.constraint i) (.var (msConstraintVars i k)) a b = false := by

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.
   532

   540				$x_4$ & $x_5$ & $x_6$ \\

   549	
   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.
   619	
   620	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]
   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622	
   623	
   624	Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\game^{\MS}$ with probability $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ is a state. Then there exist local isometries $\phi_A: \mH_A \to \mH_{A'} \otimes \mH_{A''},\phi_B: \mH_B \to \mH_{B'} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ (where $\mH_{A'},\mH_{B'} \cong (\C^2)^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mH_{A''},\mH_{B''}$ are finite dimensional) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{A''} \otimes \mH_{B''}$ such that 
   625	\begin{enumerate}
   626	    \item $\left \| \phi_A \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2} \otimes \ket{\aux} \right \| \leq O(\sqrt{\eps})$,
   627	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have that
   628	    \begin{gather*}
   629	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^X_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   630	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_b \otimes I_{B'B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\sigma^Z_b)_{A'} \otimes I_{A'' B' B''} \\
   631	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^X_b)_{B'} \\
   632	        I_{A'A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}_b    \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} I_{A' A'' B''} \otimes (\sigma^Z_b)_{B'}
   633	    \end{gather*}
   634	    where the $\approx_{\sqrt{\eps}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}_{A'B'} \otimes \ket{\aux}_{A''B''}$ and the answer summation is over $b \in \{0,1\}$. As a consequence, letting 
   635	    \begin{gather*}
   636	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1}_1 \\
   637	    \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} = \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_0 - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}_1 \\
   638	    \end{gather*}
   639	    it holds that
   640	    \begin{gather*}
   641	        \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5} \otimes I_{B' B''} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - \tilde{A}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{A}^{\Variable_1} \otimes I_{B' B''} \\
   642	        I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} - I_{A' A''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{\Variable_5}  \tilde{B}^{\Variable_1} \;,
   643	      \end{gather*}
   644	      where the notation $M \approx_{\delta} N$ for $M, N$ that are not POVM
   645	      elements means
   646	      \[  \bra{\psi} (M-N)^\dagger (M-N) \ket{\psi}  \leq  O(\delta). \]
   647	\end{enumerate}
   648	
   649	\end{theorem}
   650	\begin{proof}
   651	 	A proof of the rigidity of the Magic Square game can be found in~\cite[Theorem 6.9]{coladangelo2017robust}. There are a couple minor differences between their rigidity statement and the one stated here. First, they state that the robustness of the Magic Square self-test is $O(\eps)$; however they specify the closeness between the actual and ideal states in terms of the trace norm, whereas we specify the closeness between $\phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}\otimes \ket{\aux}$ in terms of the Euclidean distance, which translates to $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ instead of $O(\eps)$. Second, their choice of ideal strategy specifies that the observables corresponding to $\Variable_1$ and $\Variable_5$ questions are $I \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^{Z} \sigma^{X} \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$; however under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \otimes I$ and $\sigma^Z \otimes I$ respectively.
   652	\end{proof}
   653	
   654	We will need the following theorem,
   655	which shows that any pair of anticommuting observables 
   656	can be used to form a value-$1$ strategy for the Magic Square game.
   657	
   658	\begin{theorem}

1	\section{A self test for the Pauli basis}\label{sec:self-test-pauli}
     2	
     3	In this section, we give a self test for the Pauli basis measurement.
     4	Given~$W \in \{X, Z\}$, this test compels the prover
     5	to measure an EPR register in the~$W$ basis
     6	and return the outcome to the verifier.
     7	
     8	\begin{definition}
     9	The \emph{Pauli basis strategy with parameters $n$ and $q$} (a prime power),
    10	denoted $\paulistrat{n}{q}$, is the partial strategy
    11	with the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q^n}$ and measurement matrices $\tau^W_u$ for each $W \in \{X,Z\}, u \in \F_q^n$.
    12	\end{definition}
    13	
    14	The main result of this section is the following self-test for the case when~$q$ is a power of~$2$.
    15	
    16	\begin{theorem}\label{thm:basis-test}
    17	Let $\bW \sim \{X, Z\}$ uniformly at random.  Let $n$, $q$, $\eta$ satisfy the Pauli basis condition.
    18	Then there is a self-test $\game_{\mathrm{basis}} := \game_{\mathrm{basis}}(n,q)$ for $\paulistrat{n}{q}$ over~$\bW$
    19	with robustness $\delta(\eps) = \poly(\eps, \eta)$.
    20	Moreover, there is a value-$1$ real commuting EPR strategy with auxiliary state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
    21	Finally,
    22	\begin{equation*}
    23	\qlength{\game_{\mathrm{basis}}} = O\left(\log(n)\right),
    24	\quad
    25	\alength{\game_{\mathrm{basis}}} = \poly(n),
    26	\end{equation*}
    27	\begin{equation*}
    28	\qtime{\game_{\mathrm{basis}}} = O\left(\log(n)\right),
    29	\quad
    30	\atime{\game_{\mathrm{basis}}} = \poly(n).
    31	\end{equation*}
    32	\end{theorem}
    33	
    34	We prove this by a straightforward reduction to the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{NV18a}.
    35	
    36	\subsection{The quantum low-degree test}
    37	
    38	The goal of the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{NV18a}
    39	is to force the provers to use a ``compressed" version of the Pauli basis strategy.
    40	Given~$\bW$, they should measure their register in the $\bW$ basis, receiving $\bu \in \F_q^n$.
    41	However, $\bu$, a length-$n$ string, might be prohibitively expensive to communicate to the verifier,
    42	so they should instead compute the low degree encoding $g_{\bu}$
    43	and return its evaluation at a single point $\bw \in \F_q^m$ of the verifier's choosing.
    44	(The point of this section is to ``uncompress" their protocol.)
    45	
    46	\begin{definition}
    47	Fix parameters for the low-degree encoding $\params := (q = p^t, h, H, m, n, \pi)$
    48	satisfying the ``low-degree conditions"
    49	$h \leq q$, and $n \leq h^m$.
    50	For any string $u \in \F_q^n$,
    51	these parameters give a low-degree encoding $g_u:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
    52	
    53	The \emph{low-degree Pauli strategy with parameters~$\params$},
    54	denoted $\mathcal{LD}(\params)$, is the partial strategy
    55	with state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}^n_q}$ and measurement matrices
    56	\begin{equation*}
    57	\tau^{W, w}_a :=
    58	\tau^{W}_{[g_u(w) = a]} =
    59	\sum_{u : g_u(w) = a} \tau^W_u
    60	\end{equation*}
    61	for each $W \in \{X, Z\}, w \in \F_q^m, a \in \F_q$.
    62	Equivalently, this is the strategy where we perform the Pauli $W$-basis measurement
    63	and output the low-degree encoding of the outcome~$u$ evaluated at the point~$w$, i.e.\ the value $g_u(w)$.
    64	\end{definition}
    65	
    66	The main result of~\cite{NV18a} is the following.
    67	
    68	\begin{theorem}[{\cite[Theorem 3.2]{NV18a}}]\label{thm:anand-thomas-low-degree}
    69	Fix low-degree parameters~$\params$ with $p = 2$ (so that $q = 2^t$) and $m \geq 2$, 
    70	and let $\calD$ be the uniform distribution over $(W, w)$ with $W \in \{X, Z\}, w \in \F_q^m$.
    71	Then there is a self-test $\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}} := \game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}(\params)$
    72	for $\mathcal{LD}(\params)$ over~$\calD$
    73	with robustness
    74	$
    75	\delta(\epsilon) = \mathrm{poly}(\epsilon,md/q^c),
    76	$
    77	with $c > 0$.
    78	%\ainnote{TODO: Propagate to the rest of the document!!}
    79	Moreover, there is a value-$1$ real commuting EPR strategy with auxiliary state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
    80	Finally,
    81	\begin{equation*}
    82	\qlength{\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}} = O(m \log q),
    83	\quad
    84	\alength{\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}} = O(d^2 \log (q)),
    85	\end{equation*}
    86	\begin{equation*}
    87	\qtime{\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}} = O(m \log q),
    88	\quad
    89	\atime{\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}} = \poly(m, d, \log q).
    90	\end{equation*}
    91	\end{theorem}
    92	
    93	(We note that this result is stated in \cite{NV18a} for general primes~$p$.
    94	However, the $p \neq 2$ case relied on a self-testing result for a generalization of the Magic Square game
    95	which was recently discovered to contain a bug. 
    96	Fortunately, the $p=2$ case needs only a self-testing result for the
    97	``traditional" binary Magic Square game, and this follows
    98	from~\cite{WBMS16}.)
    99	
   100	\begin{remark}
   101	We note that the quantum low-degree test, as stated in \cite{NV18a}, does \emph{not} have value-$1$ real commuting EPR strategies.
   102	This is because it uses as a subroutine the standard magic square game,
   103	and the magic square game does not have value-$1$ real commuting EPR strategies.
   104	Its value-$1$ strategies \emph{are} EPR strategies,
   105	and they \emph{are} real (all observables are either $X$ or $Z$, with the sole exception of the $Y \otimes Y$ observable,
   106	which can be rewritten as $Y \otimes Y = -(X \otimes X) \cdot (Z \otimes Z)$, manifestly real).
   107	But they are not commuting, because each row and column have at least one pair of noncommuting observables.
   108	
   109	Consider instead the following ``oracularized" version of the magic square game:
   110	one player is given a random row or column (and is expected to play as in the normal magic square game),
   111	and the other player is given a random cell in that row or column,
   112	and the verifier simply checks that they agree on that cell.
   113	In addition, with some constant probability, both players are given the same cell and their answers are checked against each other.
   114	In this case, all observables measured are commuting, and so this variant has a value-$1$ real commuting EPR strategy.
   115	In addition, it certifies the same state and measurements as the normal magic square game,
   116	and so we can use it as a subroutine in the quantum low-degree test instead.
   117	\end{remark}
   118	
   119	\begin{remark}
   120	We note again that the soundness case in our definition of a self-test is quite different from the one given in \cite[Definition~$2.5$]{NV18a},
   121	and it is not clear that a self-test in their sense implies a self-test in our sense.
   122	However, for the quantum low-degree test, their soundness case \emph{does} match ours.
   123	By~\cite[Lemma~$4.1$]{NV18a}, there is a local isometry~$\phi = \phi_1 \otimes \phi_2$ such that
   124	\begin{equation}\label{eq:anand-testing-state}
   125	\Vert \phi \ket{\overline{\psi}} - \ket{\psi}\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \Vert^2 \leq \delta(\epsilon).
   126	\end{equation}
   127	and
   128	\begin{equation}\label{eq:anand-testing-state}
   129	\E_{(\bW, \bw)} \sum_a \Vert \phi \cdot (\overline{M}^{\bW, \bw}_{a} \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}) \ket{\overline{\psi}}
   130		 - (\tau_{a}^{\bW, \bw} \otimes I_{\reg{aux}})  \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}} \ket{\psi} \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \Vert^2
   131	\leq \delta(\eps).
   132	\end{equation}
   133	The key difference from our self-test definition is that, as stated, their local isometry need not be symmetric (i.e.\ $\phi_1 \neq \phi_2$),
   134	but their construction actually \emph{does} give a symmetric isometry with $\phi_1 = \phi_2$.
   135	Then, from \Cref{eq:anand-testing-state} it is easy to derive \Cref{eq:cite-once-then-never-again} using \Cref{eq:anand-testing-state} and the triangle inequality (\Cref{fact:triangle}).
   136	\end{remark}
   137	
   138	\subsection{Proof of \Cref{thm:basis-test}: the Pauli basis test}
   139	
   140	We now state the Pauli basis test.
   141	
   142	\begin{definition}
   143	Let $n,q,\eta$ be as in \Cref{thm:basis-test}.
   144	Fix the remaining low-degree parameters~$\params$ as follows:
   145	\begin{equation*}
   146	h = \lceil q^{1/2}\rceil, \qquad m = 2\cdot \left\lceil \frac{\log(n)}{\log(q)}\right\rceil,
   147	\qquad d = m \cdot (h-1).
   148	\end{equation*}
   149	Then the \emph{Pauli basis game}~$\game_{\mathrm{basis}}(n,q)$ is given by~\Cref{fig:pauli-basis}.
   150	\end{definition}
   151	
   152	{
   153	\floatstyle{boxed} 
   154	\restylefloat{figure}
   155	\begin{figure}
   156	With probability~$\tfrac{1}{2}$ each, perform one of the following two tests.
   157	\begin{enumerate}
   158	\item \textbf{Low-degree:} Perform $\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}(\params)$. \label{item:qlowdeg-test}
   159	\item \textbf{Cross-check:}  Draw $\bW \sim \{X, Z\}$, $\bw \sim \F_q^m$. Flip an unbiased coin $\bb \sim \{0, 1\}$.
   160		Distribute the questions as follows:
   161		\begin{itemize}
   162		\item[$\circ$] Player~$\bb$: Give $\bW$; receive $\bu \in \F_q^n$.
   163		\item[$\circ$] Player~$\overline{\bb}$: give $(\bW,\bw)$; receive $\ba$.
   164		\end{itemize}
   165		Accept if $g_{\bu}(\bw) = \ba$.
   166	\end{enumerate} \label{item:check-with-qlowdeg}
   167	\caption{The game $\game_{\mathrm{basis}}(n,q)$.\label{fig:pauli-basis}}
   168	\end{figure}
   169	}
   170	
   171	These parameters are chosen so that they are valid low-degree parameters
   172	(guaranteeing the existence of the low-degree code),
   173	which is necessary for the quantum low-degree test.
   174	In particular, these satisfy (i) $h \leq q$ and (ii) $n \leq h^m$.
   175	The first of these is immediate; as for the second,
   176	\begin{equation*}
   177	h^m \geq (q^{1/2})^{2 \cdot \log(n)/\log(q)} = q^{\log(n)/\log(q)} = n.
   178	\end{equation*}
   179	In addition, the code has relative distance $d/q \leq mh/q \leq \eta$.
   180	\begin{equation*}
   181	\frac{d}{q} = \frac{m \cdot(h-1)}{q} \leq \frac{m h}{q} \leq 8\cdot \frac{\log(n)}{\log(q)} \cdot \frac{q^{1/2}}{q} \leq \frac{8 \log(n)}{q^{1/2}} \leq \eta,
   182	\end{equation*}
   183	where the final step is because $n, q, \eta$ satisfy the Pauli basis condition.
   184	Finally, we note that even if~$q$ is a large polynomial of~$n$, $m$ is always at least~$2$, which permits us to use the quantum low-degree test.
   185	We now prove \Cref{thm:basis-test}.
   186	
   187	\begin{proof}[Proof of \Cref{thm:basis-test}]
   188	The question lengths and times of both the quantum low-degree test and the cross-check are given by
   189	\begin{equation*}
   190	m \log(q) = 2\cdot \left\lceil \frac{\log(n)}{\log(q)}\right\rceil  \cdot \log(q) = O(\log(n)).
   191	\end{equation*}
   192	As for the answer lengths and times, these are bounded by $\poly(n)$ for both the quantum low-degree test and the cross-check.
   193	We now consider the completeness and soundness cases separately.
   194	\paragraph{Completeness.}
   195	Let~$(\psi, M)$ be the value-$1$ commuting EPR strategy for the quantum low-degree test guaranteed by \Cref{thm:anand-thomas-low-degree}.
   196	This has state $\ket{\psi} = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q^n} \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$ and measurement matrices $M^{W,w}_a = \tau^{W,w}_a \otimes I_{\reg{aux}}$.
   197	If we add in the measurement matrices $M^W_u = \tau^W_u \otimes I_{\reg{aux}}$,
   198	then this strategy passes the cross-check with probability~$1$.
   199	This is because after Player~$\bb$ measures~$\bu$,
   200	the state collapses to $\ket{\tau^{\bW}_{\bu}}\ket{\tau^{\bW}_{\bu}} \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$,
   201	and so Player~$\overline{\bb}$ will measure $\ba = g_{\bu}(\bw)$.
   202	As a result, this is a value-$1$ strategy.
   203	Furthermore, it is a commuting EPR strategy because the cross-check measurements $M^W$ and $M^{W,w}$ commute.
   204	Finally, this strategy extends the Pauli basis strategy.
   205	This proves the completeness case.
   206	
   207	\paragraph{Soundness.}
   208	Throughout the soundness, we will use $\delta(\eps)$ to denote a function of the form $\poly(\eps, \eta)$ which may change from use to use.
   209	The $\delta(\eps)$ in \Cref{thm:anand-thomas-low-degree} is of this form because $d/q\leq \eta$.
   210	
   211	Let $\overline{\calS} = (\overline{\psi}, \overline{M})$ be a strategy with $\valstrat{\game_{\mathrm{basis}}}{\overline{\calS}} = 1-\eps$.
   212	Then this strategy must pass $\game_{\mathrm{Qlowdeg}}$ with probability at least $1-2\eps$.
   213	By \Cref{thm:anand-thomas-low-degree} this gives us a local isometry
   214	$\phi = \phi_{\mathrm{local}}\otimes \phi_{\mathrm{local}}$ and a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$
   215	with the following properties:
   216	if we define the new strategy $\calS$
   217	in which $\ket{\psi} = \phi \ket{\overline{\psi}}$
   218	and $M_a^x = \phi_{\mathrm{local}}\cdot \overline{M}_a^x \cdot \phi_{\mathrm{local}}^\dagger$, then
   219	\begin{equation}\label{eq:cant-think-of-a-good-name}
   220	\Vert \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q^n} \ket{\reg{aux}} \Vert^2 \leq \delta(\eps),
   221	\qquad
   222	M_a^{W,w} \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}
   223	\approx_{\delta(\eps)}
   224	(\tau_a^{W,w} \otimes I_{\reg{aux}}) \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}},
   225	\end{equation}
   226	on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\calD$.
   227	Because $\calS$ is just a rotated version of $\overline{\calS}$,
   228	it also passes $\game_{\mathrm{basis}}$ with probability $1-\eps$.
   229	As a result, $\calS$ passes the cross-check in \Cref{item:check-with-qlowdeg} with probability at least $1-2\eps$.
   230	By \Cref{fact:agreement}, we conclude that
   231	\begin{equation}\label{eq:worth-studying}
   232	M^W_{[g_u(w)=a]} \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}
   233	\approx_{\eps}
   234	I_{\reg{Alice}} \otimes M^{W,w}_a
   235	\approx_{\delta(\eps)} I_{\reg{Alice}} \otimes (\tau^{W,w}_a \otimes I_{\reg{aux}})
   236	= I_{\reg{Alice}} \otimes (\tau^{W}_{[g_v(w)=a]} \otimes I_{\reg{aux}})
   237	\end{equation}
   238	on state $\ket{\psi}$.
   239	By \Cref{fact:almost-agreement} and the fact that the~$\tau$ measurements are projective, this implies that
   240	\begin{equation*}
   241	M^W_{[g_u(w)=a]} \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}
   242	\consistency_{\delta(\eps)} I_{\reg{Alice}} \otimes (\tau^{W}_{[g_v(w)=a]} \otimes I_{\reg{aux}})
   243	\end{equation*}
   244	Now by
   245	\Cref{prop:same-on-point-same-on-subspace} (where we let~$\bs$ be the singleton distribution on the ``trivial" subspace $\bs = \F_q^m$)
   246	and the fact that $d/q \leq \eta$, we can conclude that
   247	\begin{equation*}
   248	M^W_{u} \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}
   249	\consistency_{\delta(\eps)} I_{\reg{Alice}} \otimes (\tau^{W}_{u} \otimes I_{\reg{aux}}).
   250	\end{equation*}
   251	Applying \Cref{fact:agreement} again, this yields
   252	\begin{equation}\label{eq:almost-there-almost-there}
   253	M_{u}^{W} \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}
   254	\approx_{\delta(\eps)} I_{\reg{Alice}} \otimes (\tau_{u}^{W} \otimes I_{\reg{aux}})
   255	\approx_{\delta(\eps)} (\tau_{u}^W \otimes I_{\reg{aux}}) \otimes I_{\reg{Bob}}
   256	\end{equation}
   257	on state $\ket{\psi}$, where the last step uses \Cref{fact:the-ol-state-y-swaperoonie}
   258	to combine \Cref{fact:the-ol-pauli-swaperoonie} with \Cref{eq:cant-think-of-a-good-name}.
   259	The analogous statement for the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q^n}$ follows from~\Cref{fact:the-ol-state-y-swaperoonie}.
   260	This establishes the theorem.

    38	/-- The 36 possible directed constraint-variable incidences. -/
    39	def directedIncidence : ((Fin 6 × Fin 3) × Bool) → MsType × MsType
    40	  | ((i, k), false) => (.constraint i, .var (msConstraintVars i k))
    41	  | ((i, k), true) => (.var (msConstraintVars i k), .constraint i)
    42	
    43	/-- Every question pair in the Magic Square distribution is a directed incidence. -/
    44	theorem ms_support_subset_directed_incidences :
    45	    (graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty).support ⊆
    46	      (Finset.univ : Finset ((Fin 6 × Fin 3) × Bool)).image directedIncidence := by
    47	  intro xy hxy
    48	  have hedge : Sym2.mk xy.1 xy.2 ∈ msEdges :=
    49	    (Finset.mem_filter.mp hxy).2
    50	  rcases Finset.mem_image.mp hedge with ⟨ik, _hik, heq⟩
    51	  have heq' :
    52	      ((.constraint ik.1, .var (msConstraintVars ik.1 ik.2)) : MsType × MsType) = xy ∨
    53	        ((.constraint ik.1, .var (msConstraintVars ik.1 ik.2)) : MsType × MsType) =
    54	          xy.swap :=
    55	    (Sym2.mk_eq_mk_iff (α := MsType)).mp heq
    56	  rcases heq' with heq' | heq'
    57	  · refine Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(ik, false), Finset.mem_univ _, ?_⟩
    58	    simpa [directedIncidence] using heq'
    59	  · refine Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(ik, true), Finset.mem_univ _, ?_⟩
    60	    simpa [directedIncidence] using congrArg Prod.swap heq'
    61	
    62	/-- The Magic Square question distribution has at most 36 support points. -/
    63	theorem ms_support_card_le :
    64	    (graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty).support.card ≤ 36 := by
    65	  calc
    66	    (graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty).support.card ≤
    67	        ((Finset.univ : Finset ((Fin 6 × Fin 3) × Bool)).image
    68	          directedIncidence).card :=
    69	      Finset.card_le_card ms_support_subset_directed_incidences
    70	    _ ≤ (Finset.univ : Finset ((Fin 6 × Fin 3) × Bool)).card :=
    71	      Finset.card_image_le
    72	    _ = 36 := by norm_num

   111	
   112	/-- The rejection mass conditioned on a question pair. -/
   113	noncomputable def rejectionMass (S : Strategy msGame) (x y : MsType) : ℝ :=
   114	  outcomeEventWeight S x y fun a b => msWinPredicate x y a b = false
   115	
   116	/-- The acceptance mass conditioned on a question pair. -/
   117	noncomputable def acceptanceMass (S : Strategy msGame) (x y : MsType) : ℝ :=
   118	  outcomeEventWeight S x y fun a b => msWinPredicate x y a b = true
   119	
   120	/-- The rejection mass averaged over the Magic Square question distribution. -/
   121	noncomputable def totalRejectionMass (S : Strategy msGame) : ℝ :=
   122	  avgOver (graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty) fun xy =>
   123	    rejectionMass S xy.1 xy.2
   124	
   125	/-- Acceptance and rejection partition the conditioned answer mass. -/

   267	answer `a` is the Naimark projection of `a`, except that the distinguished answer

   271	noncomputable def naimarkDilatedEffect {α d : Type} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   272	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] (M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement α d) (a₀ a : α) :
   273	    Op (d × Option α) :=

   280	    0 ≤ naimarkDilatedEffect M a₀ a := by

   283	  by_cases h : a = a₀

   290	    ∑ a : α, naimarkDilatedEffect M a₀ a = 1 := by

     4	/-!
     5	# A simultaneous projective dilation of a Magic Square strategy
     6	
     7	The rigidity argument for the Magic Square game is stated for an arbitrary
     8	tensor-product strategy, whose measurements are positive operator valued
     9	measures.  The self-testing argument, however, manipulates projections.  This
    10	file removes that discrepancy by dilating an arbitrary strategy to a projective
    11	one without changing any observable quantity.
    12	
    13	Each local Hilbert space `ℂ^ι` is enlarged by one auxiliary register whose
    14	basis is indexed by `Option MsAnswer`, and the original space is identified with
    15	the *ground slice* `ℂ^ι ⊗ |⊥⟩`.  The one-measurement Naimark lemma of the low
    16	individual degree development supplies, for every question separately, a family
    17	of projections on the enlarged space whose compression to the ground slice
    18	returns the original effects; the ancilla is the same for all questions, so the
    19	identification of `ℂ^ι` with the ground slice is a single isometry serving every
    20	question at once.  Folding the deficiency `1 - ∑_a P_a` into one distinguished
    21	answer turns the dilated family into a complete projective measurement without
    22	disturbing the compression, because the original effects already sum to the
    23	identity.
    24	
    25	Since the dilated state is the image of the original state under the two ground
    26	embeddings, every Born probability, and hence the game value and all the
    27	rejection, malformed-answer, cell-consistency and parity masses of the
    28	value-to-parity layer, is unchanged.  Conversely, the local isometries produced
    29	by a rigidity argument applied to the dilated strategy compose with the ground
    30	embeddings to give local isometries of the original strategy, and the
    31	state-dependent norms occurring in the conclusion of `thm:ms-rigidity` transfer
    32	along that composition.
    33	
    34	## References
    35	
    36	The rigidity statement supported here is `thm:ms-rigidity` in
    37	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`, from
    38	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:612-652`,
    39	proved in Coladangelo--Stark, Theorem 6.9.  The dilation reuses the
    40	one-measurement Naimark lemma of
    41	`references/ldt-paper/orthonormalization.tex:121-159`, formalized as
    42	`MIPStarRE.LDT.MakingMeasurementsProjective.oneMeasNaimark`.
    43	-/
    44

    54	/-! ## Orthogonality inside a subnormalized family of projections -/
    55	
    56	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`
    57	(blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`).  If an orthogonal projection `P` and a
    58	positive semidefinite operator `Q` satisfy `P + Q ≤ 1`, then `P` annihilates
    59	`Q`.  Indeed `Tr(P Q)` is nonnegative because both operators are positive
    60	semidefinite, while `0 ≤ Tr(P (1 - P - Q)) = -Tr(P Q)` because `1 - P - Q` is
    61	positive semidefinite and `P` is idempotent; so the pairing vanishes and the
    62	product of two positive semidefinite operators with vanishing trace pairing is
    63	zero. -/
    64	theorem mul_eq_zero_of_isProj_of_add_le_one {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    65	    {P Q : Op d} (hP : IsProj P) (hQ : 0 ≤ Q) (hPQ : P + Q ≤ 1) :
    66	    P * Q = 0 := by
    67	  have hrest : (0 : Op d) ≤ 1 - (P + Q) := sub_nonneg.mpr hPQ
    68	  have hexpand : P * (1 - (P + Q)) = -(P * Q) := by
    69	    have hPP : P * P = P := hP.isIdempotentElem
    70	    rw [Matrix.mul_sub, Matrix.mul_add, hPP, Matrix.mul_one]
    71	    abel
    72	  have hle : Complex.re (Matrix.trace (P * Q)) ≤ 0 := by
    73	    have h := trace_mul_nonneg_of_nonneg hP.nonneg hrest
    74	    rw [hexpand] at h
    75	    simpa using h
    76	  have hge : 0 ≤ Complex.re (Matrix.trace (P * Q)) :=
    77	    trace_mul_nonneg_of_nonneg hP.nonneg hQ
    78	  exact mul_eq_zero_of_nonneg_of_trace_mul_eq_zero hP.nonneg hQ (le_antisymm hle hge)

    80	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`
    81	(blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`).  A finite family of orthogonal
    82	projections whose sum is at most the identity is mutually orthogonal: for two
    83	distinct indices the two projections already sum to at most the identity, so the
    84	previous lemma applies. -/
    85	theorem mul_eq_zero_of_isProj_family {d α : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    86	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] {P : α → Op d} (hP : ∀ a, IsProj (P a))
    87	    (hsum : ∑ a, P a ≤ 1) {a b : α} (hab : a ≠ b) :
    88	    P a * P b = 0 := by
    89	  refine mul_eq_zero_of_isProj_of_add_le_one (hP a) (hP b).nonneg ?_
    90	  refine le_trans ?_ hsum
    91	  have hpair : ∑ c ∈ ({a, b} : Finset α), P c = P a + P b := by
    92	    rw [Finset.sum_pair hab]
    93	  rw [← hpair]
    94	  exact Finset.sum_le_sum_of_subset_of_nonneg (Finset.subset_univ _)
    95	    (fun c _ _ => (hP c).nonneg)
    96	
    97	/-- Formalization-only auxiliary lemma for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`
    98	(blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`).  The sum of a mutually orthogonal
    99	family of projections is again an orthogonal projection; mutual orthogonality is
   100	supplied by the hypothesis that the sum is at most the identity. -/
   101	theorem isProj_sum_of_isProj_of_sum_le_one {d α : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
   102	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] {P : α → Op d} (hP : ∀ a, IsProj (P a))
   103	    (hsum : ∑ a, P a ≤ 1) :
   104	    IsProj (∑ a, P a) := by
   105	  constructor
   106	  · show (∑ a, P a) * (∑ a, P a) = ∑ a, P a

   122	point.  Formalization-only support for the dilation used by `thm:ms-rigidity`,
   123	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`. -/
   124	def naimarkEmbeddingMap (ι α : Type) [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   125	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] :
   126	    EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ (ι × Option α) where
   127	  toFun x := (EuclideanSpace.equiv (ι × Option α) ℂ).symm
   128	    (fun p => if p.2 = none then x p.1 else 0)
   129	  map_add' x y := by
   130	    ext p
   131	    by_cases h : p.2 = none <;> simp [h]
   132	  map_smul' c x := by
   133	    ext p
   134	    by_cases h : p.2 = none <;> simp [h]

   136	/-- The isometric identification of a local Hilbert space `ℂ^ι` with the *ground
   137	slice* `ℂ^ι ⊗ |⊥⟩` of the enlarged space `ℂ^{ι × Option α}`.  This single
   138	embedding serves every question of the dilation supporting `thm:ms-rigidity`,
   139	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`, paper
   140	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:612-652`. -/
   141	noncomputable def naimarkEmbedding (ι α : Type) [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   142	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] :
   143	    EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ (ι × Option α) :=
   144	  LinearMap.isometryOfInner (naimarkEmbeddingMap ι α) <| by
   145	    intro x y
   146	    simp [PiLp.inner_apply, Fintype.sum_prod_type, naimarkEmbeddingMap]

   148	/-- The coordinates of the ground embedding: the amplitude is carried to the
   149	auxiliary basis vector `|⊥⟩` and vanishes on the other auxiliary vectors. -/
   150	@[simp]
   151	theorem naimarkEmbedding_apply {ι α : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   152	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) (p : ι × Option α) :
   153	    naimarkEmbedding ι α x p = if p.2 = none then x p.1 else 0 := rfl
   154	
   155	/-- The compression of an operator on the enlarged space to the ground slice.
   156	Formalization-only support for the dilation of `thm:ms-rigidity`, blueprint
   157	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`. -/
   158	def naimarkCompression {ι α : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   159	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (M : Op (ι × Option α)) : Op ι :=
   160	  M.submatrix (fun i => (i, none)) (fun j => (j, none))
   161	
   162	/-- The entries of the ground-slice compression. -/
   163	@[simp]
   164	theorem naimarkCompression_apply {ι α : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   165	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (M : Op (ι × Option α)) (i j : ι) :
   166	    naimarkCompression (α := α) M i j = M (i, none) (j, none) := rfl
   167	
   168	/-- The compression of the zero operator to the ground slice vanishes. -/
   169	@[simp]
   170	theorem naimarkCompression_zero {ι α : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   171	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] :
   172	    naimarkCompression (α := α) (0 : Op (ι × Option α)) = 0 := by
   173	  ext i j; simp
   174	
   175	/-- The compression to the ground slice is additive. -/
   176	theorem naimarkCompression_add {ι α : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   177	    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (M N : Op (ι × Option α)) :
   178	    naimarkCompression (α := α) (M + N) =
   179	      naimarkCompression (α := α) M + naimarkCompression (α := α) N := by
   180	  ext i j; simp

   381	theorem naimarkDilatedState_apply (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   382	    {ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
   383	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) (p : (ιA × Option α) × (ιB × Option α)) :
   384	    naimarkDilatedState α ψ p =
   385	      if p.1.2 = none ∧ p.2.2 = none then ψ (p.1.1, p.2.1) else 0 := by

   387	  obtain ⟨⟨i, oa⟩, ⟨j, ob⟩⟩ := p
   388	  simp only [naimarkDilatedState, isometryTensor]
   389	  by_cases hoa : oa = none

   398	theorem inner_applyOperatorToState {ι : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]

   408	    {ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
   409	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) (i : ιA) (oa : Option α) (j : ιB) (ob : Option α) :

references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:651: 	A proof of the rigidity of the Magic Square game can be found in~\cite[Theorem 6.9]{coladangelo2017robust}. There are a couple minor differences between their rigidity statement and the one stated here. First, they state that the robustness of the Magic Square self-test is $O(\eps)$; however they specify the closeness between the actual and ideal states in terms of the trace norm, whereas we specify the closeness between $\phi_\alice \otimes \phi_\bob \ket{\psi}$ and $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes 2}\otimes \ket{\aux}$ in terms of the Euclidean distance, which translates to $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ instead of $O(\eps)$. Second, their choice of ideal strategy specifies that the observables corresponding to $\Variable_1$ and $\Variable_5$ questions are $I \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\sigma^{Z} \sigma^{X} \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$; however under a local change of basis these are equivalent to $\sigma^X \otimes I$ and $\sigma^Z \otimes I$ respectively.

+/-- Conjugating an operator by the ground embedding followed by a later local
+isometry is conjugating its inflation by that isometry.  This is the form in
+which the conclusions of a self-testing argument applied to the dilated strategy
+are read back on the original strategy. -/
+theorem conjIsometry_comp_naimarkEmbedding {ι α κ : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ]
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ι × Option α) →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κ) (M : Op ι) :
+    conjIsometry (φ.comp (naimarkEmbedding ι α)) M =
+      conjIsometry φ (naimarkInflation (α := α) M) := by
+  rw [conjIsometry_comp, conjIsometry_naimarkEmbedding]
+
+/-- Compressing one of Alice's dilated Magic Square effects to the ground slice
+returns her original effect. -/
+theorem naimarkCompression_msDilatedStrategy_A_effect (S : Strategy msGame)
+    (x : MsType) (a : MsAnswer) :
+    naimarkCompression (α := MsAnswer) (((msDilatedStrategy S).A x).effect a) =
+      (S.A x).effect a :=
+  naimarkCompression_naimarkDilatedEffect (α := MsAnswer) (S.A x) (MsAnswer.bit 0) a
+
+/-- Compressing one of Bob's dilated Magic Square effects to the ground slice
+returns his original effect. -/
+theorem naimarkCompression_msDilatedStrategy_B_effect (S : Strategy msGame)
+    (y : MsType) (b : MsAnswer) :
+    naimarkCompression (α := MsAnswer) (((msDilatedStrategy S).B y).effect b) =
+      (S.B y).effect b :=
+  naimarkCompression_naimarkDilatedEffect (α := MsAnswer) (S.B y) (MsAnswer.bit 0) b
+

+/-- The matrix of a linear isometry of Euclidean spaces in the computational
+bases.  Formalization-only support for `thm:ms-rigidity`, blueprint
+`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`. -/
+noncomputable def isometryMatrix {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') : Matrix ι' ι ℂ :=
+  Matrix.toEuclideanLin.symm φ.toLinearMap
+
+/-- Conjugation by an isometry is conjugation by its matrix. -/
+theorem conjIsometry_eq {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') (M : Op ι) :
+    conjIsometry φ M = isometryMatrix φ * M * (isometryMatrix φ)ᴴ := rfl
+
+/-- The matrix of an isometry acts on vectors as the isometry does. -/
+theorem isometryMatrix_mulVec {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') (x : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) :
+    isometryMatrix φ *ᵥ WithLp.ofLp x = WithLp.ofLp (φ x) := by
+  have h : Matrix.toEuclideanLin (isometryMatrix φ) = φ.toLinearMap :=
+    Matrix.toEuclideanLin.apply_symm_apply φ.toLinearMap
+  have h' : Matrix.toEuclideanLin (isometryMatrix φ) x = φ x := by rw [h]; rfl
+  simpa using congrArg WithLp.ofLp h'
+
+/-- The columns of the matrix of an isometry are the images of the basis
+vectors. -/
+theorem isometryMatrix_apply {ι ι' : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι') (k : ι') (i : ι) :
+    isometryMatrix φ k i =
+      φ ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1)) k := by
+  have h := congrFun (isometryMatrix_mulVec φ
+    ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1))) k
+  rw [← h]
+  simp [Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct, EuclideanSpace.equiv, eq_comm]
+
+/-- The matrix of a composite isometry is the product of the two matrices. -/
+theorem isometryMatrix_comp {ι κ ν : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ] [Fintype ν] [DecidableEq ν]
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ κ →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ν)
+    (E : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κ) :
+    isometryMatrix (φ.comp E) = isometryMatrix φ * isometryMatrix E := by
+  ext k i
+  have h := congrFun (isometryMatrix_mulVec φ
+    (E ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1)))) k
+  rw [isometryMatrix_apply, Matrix.mul_apply]
+  simp only [isometryMatrix_apply E]
+  simpa [Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct] using h.symm

+`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`. -/
+theorem conjIsometry_comp {ι κ ν : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype κ] [DecidableEq κ] [Fintype ν] [DecidableEq ν]
+    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ κ →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ν)
+    (E : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κ) (M : Op ι) :
+    conjIsometry (φ.comp E) M = conjIsometry φ (conjIsometry E M) := by
+  rw [conjIsometry_eq, conjIsometry_eq, conjIsometry_eq, isometryMatrix_comp]

+    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κB)

+theorem isometryTensor_comp {ιA ιB κA κB νA νB : Type}
+    [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
+    [Fintype κA] [DecidableEq κA] [Fintype κB] [DecidableEq κB]
+    [Fintype νA] [DecidableEq νA] [Fintype νB] [DecidableEq νB]
+    (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ κA →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ νA)
+    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ κB →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ νB)
+    (EA : EuclideanSpace ℂ ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κA)
+    (EB : EuclideanSpace ℂ ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κB)
+    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
+    isometryTensor (φA.comp EA) (φB.comp EB) ψ =
+      isometryTensor φA φB (isometryTensor EA EB ψ) := by
+  ext p
+  rw [isometryTensor_apply_eq, isometryTensor_apply_eq]
+  simp only [isometryTensor_apply_eq, isometryMatrix_comp, Finset.mul_sum]
+  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
+  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun r _ => ?_
+  have hk : (isometryMatrix φA * isometryMatrix EA).kronecker
+        (isometryMatrix φB * isometryMatrix EB) =
+      (isometryMatrix φA).kronecker (isometryMatrix φB) *
+        (isometryMatrix EA).kronecker (isometryMatrix EB) :=
+    Matrix.mul_kronecker_mul _ _ _ _
+  rw [hk, Matrix.mul_apply, Finset.sum_mul]
+  exact Finset.sum_congr rfl fun x _ => by ring
+
+/-- The ground embeddings of the dilation composed with two later local
+isometries carry the original state exactly as those isometries carry the
+dilated state. -/
+theorem isometryTensor_comp_naimarkEmbedding (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    {ιA ιB κA κB : Type} [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
+    [Fintype κA] [DecidableEq κA] [Fintype κB] [DecidableEq κB]
+    (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × Option α) →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κA)
+    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB × Option α) →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ κB)
+    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
+    isometryTensor (φA.comp (naimarkEmbedding ιA α)) (φB.comp (naimarkEmbedding ιB α)) ψ =
+      isometryTensor φA φB (naimarkDilatedState α ψ) :=
+  isometryTensor_comp φA φB _ _ ψ
+
+/-! ## Transfer of state-dependent bounds -/
+
+/-- Conjugating an operator by the ground embedding inflates it: the result acts
+as the original operator on the ground slice and annihilates the orthogonal
+complement. -/
+theorem conjIsometry_naimarkEmbedding {ι α : Type} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] (M : Op ι) :
+    conjIsometry (naimarkEmbedding ι α) M = naimarkInflation (α := α) M := by
+  ext p q
+  rw [conjIsometry_eq]
+  simp only [Matrix.mul_apply, Matrix.conjTranspose_apply, isometryMatrix_apply,
+    naimarkEmbedding_apply, naimarkInflation_apply, EuclideanSpace.equiv]
+  by_cases hp : p.2 = none
+  · by_cases hq : q.2 = none <;> simp [hp, hq, eq_comm]
+  · simp [hp]
+
+/-- The action of an operator on the dilated state only sees its ground-slice
+columns. -/
+theorem applyOperatorToState_naimarkDilatedState (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    {ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
+    (K : Op ((ιA × Option α) × (ιB × Option α)))
+    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) (p : (ιA × Option α) × (ιB × Option α)) :
+    applyOperatorToState K (naimarkDilatedState α ψ) p =
+      ∑ k : ιA, ∑ l : ιB, K p ((k, none), (l, none)) * ψ (k, l) := by
+  classical
+  simp [applyOperatorToState, Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct, Fintype.sum_prod_type,
+    Fintype.sum_option, naimarkDilatedState_apply_mul]
+
+/-- Inflated operators act on the dilated state exactly as the original
+operators act on the original state.  This is the identity that transfers
+state-dependent effect bounds back to the undilated strategy. -/
+theorem applyOperatorToState_heteroKron_naimarkInflation
+    (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    {ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
+    (M : Op ιA) (N : Op ιB) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
+    applyOperatorToState
+        (heteroKron (naimarkInflation (α := α) M) (naimarkInflation (α := α) N))
+        (naimarkDilatedState α ψ) =
+      naimarkDilatedState α (applyOperatorToState (heteroKron M N) ψ) := by
+  classical
+  ext p
+  rw [applyOperatorToState_naimarkDilatedState, naimarkDilatedState_apply]
+  obtain ⟨⟨i, oa⟩, ⟨j, ob⟩⟩ := p
+  by_cases hoa : oa = none
+  · by_cases hob : ob = none
+    · simp [hoa, hob, heteroKron, applyOperatorToState, Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct,
+        Fintype.sum_prod_type, mul_assoc]
+    · simp [hob, heteroKron]
+  · simp [hoa, heteroKron]
+
+/-- The state-dependent norm of an inflated operator on the dilated state equals
+the state-dependent norm of the original operator on the original state. -/
+theorem norm_applyOperatorToState_heteroKron_naimarkInflation
+    (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    {ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
+    (M : Op ιA) (N : Op ιB) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
+    ‖applyOperatorToState
+        (heteroKron (naimarkInflation (α := α) M) (naimarkInflation (α := α) N))
+        (naimarkDilatedState α ψ)‖ =
+      ‖applyOperatorToState (heteroKron M N) ψ‖ := by
+  rw [applyOperatorToState_heteroKron_naimarkInflation, naimarkDilatedState_norm]
+
+/-- Transfer of state-dependent effect bounds.  Every average squared distance
+between two families of inflated operators, measured on the dilated state, is
+the corresponding distance between the original families measured on the
+original state; a bound obtained for the dilated strategy is therefore a bound
+for the strategy one started from.  Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:224-253`,
+paper `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:612-652`. -/
+theorem opFamilyDistSq_naimarkInflation (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
+    {X γ ιA ιB : Type} [Fintype γ] [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA]
+    [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
+    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → γ → Op ιA) (P : X → γ → Op ιB)
+    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
+    opFamilyDistSq μ
+        (fun x c => heteroKron (naimarkInflation (α := α) (M x c))
+          (naimarkInflation (α := α) (P x c)))
+        (fun x c => heteroKron (naimarkInflation (α := α) (N x c))
+          (naimarkInflation (α := α) (P x c)))
+        (naimarkDilatedState α ψ) =
+      opFamilyDistSq μ (fun x c => heteroKron (M x c) (P x c))
+        (fun x c => heteroKron (N x c) (P x c)) ψ := by
+  unfold opFamilyDistSq
+  congr 1
+  funext x
+  refine Finset.sum_congr rfl fun c _ => ?_
+  have hkron : ∀ {ρA ρB : Type} [Fintype ρA] [DecidableEq ρA] [Fintype ρB] [DecidableEq ρB]
+      (X Y : Op ρA) (Z : Op ρB),
+      heteroKron X Z - heteroKron Y Z = heteroKron (X - Y) Z := by
+    intro ρA ρB _ _ _ _ X Y Z
+    ext p q
+    simp [heteroKron, Matrix.kronecker, sub_mul]
+  have hinfl : naimarkInflation (α := α) (M x c) - naimarkInflation (α := α) (N x c) =
+      naimarkInflation (α := α) (M x c - N x c) := by
+    ext p q
+    by_cases h : p.2 = none ∧ q.2 = none <;> simp [h]
+  rw [hkron, hkron, hinfl, norm_applyOperatorToState_heteroKron_naimarkInflation]
+

references/cs-paper/Arxiv v2 - Robust LCS self testing/introduction.tex:3:If we pick any row and take the product of the three operators in that row (note that they commute, so the order does not matter), we get the identity operator. Similarly, we can try this with the columns. Two of the columns give identity while the other  gives $-1$ times identity. Thus, the product of these nine operators depends on whether they are multiplied row by row or column by column. This can be exploited to define a two-player, one-referee game called the Mermin--Peres Magic Square game \cite{aravind2004quantum} (see Definition \ref{definition:linear-constraint-game} and Figure \ref{fig:magic-square-equations} for a formal definition). Informally, the Mermin--Peres Magic Square game mod $2$ is as follows. The players claim to have a $3\times 3$ square of numbers in which each row and each of the first two columns sums to $0\pmod 2$, while the third column sums to $1\pmod 2$. (The players are usually called ``provers'', since they try to prove that they have such a square.) The referee asks the first player to present a row of the supposed square and the second to present a column. They reply respectively with the $3$ entries of that row and column in $\{0,1\}$. They win if their responses sum to $0$ or $1$ as appropriate, and they give the same number for the entry where the row and column overlap. This game can be won with probability $1$ by provers that share two pairs of maximally entangled qubits of dimension $2$, but provers with no entanglement can win with probability at most $\frac89$. Games which are won in the classical case with probability $< 1$ but are won in the quantum case with probability $1$ are known as \emph{pseudotelepathy games}.
